#9006. The GLP Coaching Institute Certification: Frequently Asked Questions

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a comprehensive professional education program developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute in partnership with Precision Nutrition. It combines GLP-1 science with evidence-based behaviour-change methods and practical coaching skills to help health, fitness, nutrition, and medical professionals better support clients using GLP-1 medications.

GLP-1 medications are changing the way clients eat, exercise, and recover. And many professionals are facing questions their existing education hasn’t fully prepared them to answer.

This certification helps close that gap, with specialized training in GLP-1 physiology, nutrition, exercise, recovery, and coaching. From navigating reduced appetite and protecting strength to supporting long-term maintenance, you’ll use the Five GLP Types to decide where to start and learn how to adapt your approach to the person in front of you.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a comprehensive professional education program that prepares health, fitness, and medical professionals to support clients using GLP-1 medications.

Developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute in partnership with Precision Nutrition, the certification combines GLP-1 science, evidence-based behavior-change methods, and practical coaching skills in one complete program.

Across four units and 30 chapters, you’ll learn how GLP-1 medications affect the body, how to adapt nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies to your clients’ changing needs, and how to apply a structured coaching process throughout treatment.

You’ll also develop the professional skills to work effectively alongside a client’s medical team and build a GLP-1 coaching practice.

Upon successful completion, you’ll earn the Certified GLP Coaching Specialist (CGCS) credential.

GLP-1 medications change how the body regulates appetite, weight, and energy. That means the nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies professionals typically use may need to change, too.

For example, a client with a dramatically reduced appetite may struggle to get enough protein and essential nutrients. Someone who’s losing weight quickly may also be losing strength or struggling to recover from workouts that used to feel manageable.

Others may experience medication-related side effects, changes in their relationship with food, or plateaus that require a different approach.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

It also means recognizing when a client’s needs go beyond coaching and require input from their prescriber or another healthcare professional.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification was developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute, in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

Dr. Berardi is the co-founder of Precision Nutrition and founder of the GLP Coaching Institute. He holds a PhD in exercise physiology and nutritional biochemistry and is a Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist (CSCS). With more than 30 years of experience as a scientist, educator, and coach, he’s helped shape nutrition and health coaching education worldwide.

The GLP Coaching Institute brings specialized expertise in supporting people using GLP-1 medications, including the Five GLP Types framework.

Precision Nutrition contributes more than 20 years of experience in coaching education, behavior change, and its proven coaching methodology, which has helped train and support more than 350,000 clients, coaches, and clinicians worldwide.

Together, they’ve created a standalone professional certification that combines GLP-1 science with practical, evidence-based coaching education.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification goes beyond teaching you how GLP-1 medications work. It teaches you how to turn that knowledge into effective, individualized coaching.

The curriculum combines in-depth GLP-1 science with Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology and practical strategies designed specifically for people using these medications.

You’ll learn how to assess clients, identify their most pressing needs using the Five GLP Types, prioritize interventions, and adjust your approach as their circumstances change.

You’ll also work through real-world client cases and practical activities that help you apply what you’re learning, from building nutrition and exercise plans to navigating plateaus, supporting long-term maintenance, and collaborating with healthcare providers.

And because coaching doesn’t stop at the client session, the certification also covers how to develop your GLP-1 coaching services, build professional referral relationships, and communicate your expertise responsibly.

Yes. The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is grounded in current scientific research and evidence-based behavior-change principles, combined with practical coaching frameworks developed through years of professional experience.

The curriculum draws on research in obesity, weight regulation, GLP-1 pharmacology, nutrition, exercise, recovery, and behavior change.

Throughout the program, you’ll learn what the research supports, where evidence is still emerging, and how to evaluate new claims in a rapidly changing field.

The certification also incorporates Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology and the Five GLP Types, a framework for identifying and prioritizing individual coaching needs.

These are practitioner frameworks informed by science and coaching experience, not medical diagnostic tools or interventions independently validated through clinical trials.

The goal is to help you make informed coaching decisions, communicate accurately with clients, and recognize when questions or concerns require medical expertise.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is designed for health, fitness, nutrition, and medical professionals who work with, or want to work with, people using GLP-1 medications.

That includes health and nutrition coaches, personal trainers, strength coaches, registered dietitians, physicians, nurses, and other allied health professionals.

You don’t need a clinical background to enroll. The certification teaches the science of GLP-1 medications in accessible language, then shows you how to apply that knowledge within your professional role.

Whether you’re working in a gym, private coaching practice, or healthcare setting, you’ll learn how to better support GLP-1 clients and collaborate with their medical team.

The certification does not expand your existing professional scope of practice.

Yes. You don’t need to be working with GLP-1 clients to benefit from the certification.

GLP-1 medications are becoming increasingly common, and more health and fitness professionals are encountering clients who use them.

In our 2026 survey of 2,490 health and fitness professionals, 65.1% reported already working with GLP-1 clients, compared with 45.8% in our 2024 survey.

This certification helps you prepare for the questions these clients may bring, from navigating reduced appetite and maintaining muscle to adapting workouts and supporting long-term health.

You’ll develop the knowledge and practical skills to work with this population before those questions arise in your own practice.

If you’re already working with GLP-1 clients, the certification will help you build on your existing skills with GLP-specific science, tools, and coaching strategies.

You may already be helping clients adjust their nutrition, maintain strength, or manage changes in energy and recovery. But GLP-1 treatment introduces challenges that traditional coaching education doesn’t always address.

You’ll deepen your understanding of the physiology behind those challenges and learn a structured approach to assessing clients, identifying priorities, adapting interventions, and measuring progress.

Through practical activities and client case studies, you’ll have opportunities to apply what you’re learning to real-world situations, including complex cases where several challenges need attention at once.

The result is a more informed, systematic approach to supporting GLP-1 clients, rather than having to figure out each new situation as it comes.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification provides comprehensive training in GLP-1 science, nutrition, exercise, recovery, behavior change, and professional coaching. Across four units and 30 chapters, you’ll learn how GLP-1 medications affect the body and how to adapt your coaching to the specific needs of clients using them.

Throughout the certification, you’ll work with practical activities, coaching tools, and client case studies designed to help you apply your learning.

The Five GLP Types are a coaching assessment and prioritization framework developed by Dr. John Berardi to help professionals identify a GLP-1 client’s most pressing challenges and decide where to focus first.

Each Type represents a different area where a client may need additional support.

Clients may experience challenges across several Types, and their priorities can change over time.

The framework helps you identify where to start, choose appropriate coaching strategies, and adjust your approach as your client’s needs change.

The Five GLP Types are not medical diagnoses. They’re practical tools for organizing coaching decisions, used alongside Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology.

After completing the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, you’ll have the knowledge, tools, and practical skills to assess GLP-1 clients, develop individualized coaching strategies, and adapt your approach as their needs change throughout treatment.

You’ll practice these skills through client case studies and a culminating project that brings the full coaching process together.

The goal isn’t simply to know more about GLP-1 medications. It’s to develop the practical judgment to apply that knowledge to the clients and situations you’ll encounter in your work.

Yes. The certification includes in-depth education on how GLP-1 medications work, how different medications affect the body, common side effects, and the physiological changes that can occur during treatment.

You’ll learn how to recognize medication-related challenges that affect nutrition, exercise, and recovery, and how to adapt your coaching appropriately.

However, this is a coaching certification, not a license to prescribe or manage GLP-1 medications.

Medication decisions, including starting, stopping, or adjusting treatment, remain the responsibility of the client and their prescribing healthcare professional.

Your coaching role may include helping clients meet their nutrition needs, maintain strength and function, build sustainable habits, and prepare for changes in their treatment plan.

You’ll also learn to recognize when symptoms or concerns require referral and how to collaborate effectively with a client’s medical team.

Your professional scope of practice depends on your existing qualifications and the regulations in your jurisdiction. Completing this certification does not expand that scope.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a standalone specialty certification focused specifically on supporting people using GLP-1 medications. It complements Precision Nutrition’s existing certifications rather than replacing them.

Each program serves a different educational purpose:

Already completed the GLP-1 chapter in PN Level 1?

The GLP-1 chapter in Level 1 introduces how GLP-1 medications work, what clients may experience, and how nutrition coaching may need to adapt.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification takes that foundation much further. With approximately 80 hours of dedicated education, you’ll develop a deeper understanding of GLP-1 physiology and learn specific strategies for nutrition, exercise, recovery, and long-term maintenance.

You’ll also learn a structured GLP-1 coaching process, including the Five GLP Types, and apply your knowledge through client case studies and a culminating project.

If you’re already PN-certified, the underlying coaching methodology will be familiar. What’s new is how you’ll apply it to the unique needs and challenges of GLP-1 clients.

Looking for GLP-1 coaching for yourself? This certification is designed for professionals. If you’re taking a GLP-1 medication and looking for personalized support, explore the coaching programs available through the GLP Coaching Institute.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification takes approximately 80 hours to complete and is 100% online and self-paced, so you can work through the material on your own schedule.

The certification is delivered through Precision Nutrition’s online learning platform and includes four units and 30 chapters.

You can work through the certification at a pace that fits your schedule, whether you’re balancing a full client roster, another job, or other commitments.

No. There are no prerequisites for the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, and you don’t need to have completed another Precision Nutrition certification.

The program teaches the foundational science, coaching methodology, and GLP-specific strategies you’ll need, so professionals from different health, fitness, and medical backgrounds can complete the training.

If you’re already PN-certified, you’ll recognize elements of Precision Nutrition’s coaching approach while learning how to apply them specifically to clients using GLP-1 medications.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification combines open-book chapter exams with a practical culminating project designed to assess how well you understand and apply what you’ve learned.

Each of the 30 chapters includes a 10-question, multiple-choice exam. You’ll need a cumulative score of at least 75% across the chapter exams to pass.

There is no separate cumulative final exam.

Instead, you’ll complete a culminating project in which you assess a GLP-1 client, identify their coaching priorities, develop an individualized plan, and explain the reasoning behind your recommendations.

This final project brings together the science, coaching methodology, and practical skills taught throughout the certification.

After successfully completing the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, you’ll earn the designation Certified GLP Coaching Specialist (CGCS), issued by the GLP Coaching Institute.

This credential recognizes your completion of specialized professional education in supporting clients using GLP-1 medications.

The certification will include a renewal process to help professionals stay current as GLP-1 science and coaching practices evolve.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is being developed with continuing education requirements in mind, and applications for continuing education recognition are planned.

The curriculum includes defined learning objectives, assessments, and documented educational content to support applications for continuing education credits.

Approvals and the number of credits available will depend on the relevant professional organizations.

#9003. 8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

But the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health issues (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you plan to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is currently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.)

With 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”

The flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

#9002. 12-Minute Calming Yoga to Gently Ease You Into Relaxation Mode

Ebony Smith, yoga instructor and founder of Yoga N Da Hood, offers a quick yin yoga practice to soothe the body and mind when you’re feeling anxious, overwhelmed, or simply need a break.

Even if anxiety is something you experience on the regular, you know that it can show up in completely expected ways throughout the day. Maybe you mentally replay a situation you wish you’d handled differently, or feel a sense of urgency to make more than one huge life decision in a single afternoon.

Yet sometimes the surest way to connect with yourself amid anxious tendencies is turning your attention to something that takes place in the here and now, rather than relates to the past or future. Such as stepping onto your yoga mat.

The following yin yoga practice is designed to help you relax and release tension, especially in your hips and lower back, by anchoring your body into the present moment—which can also encourage your mind to do the same. It’s a simple stretching practice that is quite restorative, especially when you feel apprehensive during the day or when you need some soothing before bed.

This sequence is made of supported yin yoga poses, slow breaths, and intentional pauses. No yoga experience needed. Simply find as quiet of a space as you can and, if possible, dim the lights. You can use a pillow, bolster, or block for extra support. Most yin yoga poses ask you to remain still for 3 to 5 minutes to create a stretch in the connective tissues. However, you can rest here for shorter amounts of time.

A little supine twist to get the party started. Lie on your back with your feet flat on the mat and your knees shining toward the ceiling. Take your arms straight out to the sides. Keep your feet on the mat as you lower both knees over toward the right. Turn your gaze over your left shoulder.

Stay here or, if it feels good, cross your left leg over your right. You can also place your right hand on your left thigh to gently intensify the stretch. To lessen the intensity, you can slide a pillow or bolster underneath your left knee. Notice where you might be holding any tension from the day and see if you can release it. Rest here for up to 3 minutes, then switch sides.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Rest your arms by your sides and roll your shoulders underneath you. When you’re ready, press your feet into the mat and lift your hips toward the ceiling. Slide your block or bolster or pillows underneath your sacrum (the lowest part of your spine) in Supported Bridge Pose. Find a comfortable position, then rest here.

When you’re ready, remove the prop underneath you and lower your hips to the mat. Gently windshield wiper your knees side to side a few times.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Take your feet wider, so they’re at the edge of the mat or a little outside the mat. Then relax your knees toward each other. They might rest against one another and they might not. Find a position in which you don’t have to use your muscles to hold your legs and you’re using gravity to draw your knees together. Take your arms out to the side or rest one hand over your heart and the other on your belly. Close your eyes if it feels good. Rest here.

From Constructive Rest, extend your legs long on the mat, maybe wiggling them out before finding stillness. Rest your arms by your sides. If it feels good, you can spread your palms out wide, shining them toward the ceiling. Close your eyes and begin to allow any stress, any worries, any fears, any doubts to melt off of you in Savasana. Notice yourself breathing in and out.

You can stay in Savasana for as long as it serves you. When you’re ready to come out of it, maybe wiggle your toes and fingers and stretch your arms overhead. Awaken to the amazing human being you truly are.

#9001. The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

You might find a few surprising advantages of cycling on this list.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

“Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

While almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” says Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance issues.”

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he says.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

“As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

You can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

“By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a big deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These issues can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an important undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

“Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

Whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

In fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

One area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more quickly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” says Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”

This isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health issues,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

Cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” says Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

In fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins

Here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart currently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

What you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:

All transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

This is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. For the best seat selection and availability, aim to search within that window as early as possible.

Delta SkyMiles uses fully dynamic pricing with no published award chart, meaning business class awards can range from 80,000 to 500,000 SkyMiles for the same route depending on demand. Virgin Atlantic, as a Delta joint venture partner, maintains a fixed award chart for Delta-operated flights — creating a massive pricing arbitrage. A JFK-to-London Delta One Suite that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles can often be booked through Virgin for 47,500 Flying Club miles. Both programs see the same award inventory, but Virgin prices it using their distance-based chart instead of Delta's demand-based algorithm. Since Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club accepts 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, you can earn these miles through credit card spending without ever flying Virgin Atlantic.

The Route: New York JFK → Los Angeles LAX The Aircraft: Airbus A350-900 The Cabin: Delta One Suites

Pull up Delta.com on a typical travel date and you'll find Delta One Suites on this route priced anywhere from $2,500 for a off-peak weekday to $5,000–$6,000 during peak summer weekends or holiday travel. The five-hour flight from New York to Los Angeles becomes an experience rather than a commute. You arrive rested, full, and having spent roughly $11 out of pocket on a seat your fellow passengers paid $3,500 for. That gap — that's the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in action.

Delta One availability on high-demand routes like JFK–LAX is not unlimited — it's released in waves and often fills quickly for peak dates. Set a calendar reminder to search exactly 331 days before your target travel date. This is especially important for holiday travel, summer weekends, and any dates where you have a hard deadline.

Since transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are instant, you can do a same-call transfer — confirm availability with the agent, ask them to hold for a moment, transfer your points in a separate browser tab, and confirm with the agent that the miles have landed. This eliminates the risk of availability disappearing between your transfer and your booking attempt.

While this sweet spot is available year-round, Delta One availability is generally better on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday departures when leisure demand is lower. If your travel dates are flexible, searching across a week of dates will often surface better availability on midweek flights.

Virgin Atlantic's award chart has high fuel surcharges on Virgin Atlantic-operated flights. This guide is specifically about Delta-operated flights. Never confuse the two. When you call to book, confirm the operating carrier is Delta. The surcharge-free benefit applies only to partner awards.

Points transfers are irreversible. A common and painful mistake is transferring points to Flying Club only to discover the specific flight you wanted has no award availability. Always confirm availability verbally with a Flying Club agent before initiating any transfer.

The most efficient path to 50,000 points is a single credit card welcome bonus. The Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Sapphire Reserve both offer welcome bonuses that can fully fund this redemption — and both transfer to Virgin Atlantic at 1:1 instantly. Alternatively, the Amex Gold Card or Platinum Card welcome bonuses work equally well via Amex's instant transfer path.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A simple fix: make a small earning transaction (even a hotel stay or car rental through their partners) at least once every three years.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want a genuinely luxurious experience on one of America's premier transcontinental routes and are comfortable with a moderate amount of booking complexity — primarily a phone call to Virgin Atlantic.

Minimum points needed: 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person (100,000 for two). These are most efficiently sourced via a single credit card welcome bonus.

For the FI-minded traveler who has earned a moderate points balance and wants to experience premium cabin travel on a meaningful domestic route, this is a standout use of currency. The 5–12 CPP range makes it one of the most efficient domestic business class redemptions available.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — not because any individual step is technically complex, but because it requires coordinating two separate systems (Delta.com for availability searching and Virgin Atlantic by phone for booking) and making an irreversible transfer decision under some time pressure. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Availability is the main hurdle.** Delta One award inventory released to partners is limited, particularly on peak dates. You won't always find seats when you want them, and the 331-day booking window means planning further ahead than most travelers are accustomed to. 2. **The booking requires a phone call.** There's no self-service online booking for Virgin Atlantic partner awards. Some travelers find this intimidating; in practice, Flying Club agents are helpful and accustomed to partner award bookings. 3. **The transfer-before-booking sequence requires discipline.** The rule is: confirm first, transfer second. Getting that order wrong is an expensive mistake. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use Delta.com as your search engine.** It shows real-time award availability far more reliably than third-party tools for Delta-operated flights. - **Call Virgin Atlantic during off-peak hours** (early morning Eastern time tends to mean shorter hold times and more patient agents). - **Have your flight details written down** before you call — flight number, date, origin, destination, and Flying Club number. A prepared caller gets a faster, smoother booking. If you've ever transferred points to an airline program and called to book an award, this process will feel completely familiar. If this is your first partner award booking, treat it as a learning experience — the 5–12 CPP reward on the other side is well worth one phone call.

Log into your Delta SkyMiles account and search for one-way business class (Delta One) award flights. Filter for nonstop flights on the A350-900, which is the aircraft with Delta One Suites. Note the dates that show availability — this is the same inventory Virgin can book.

If you do not already have a Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, create one at virginatlantic.com. You need an active account to receive transferred miles and to reference when calling to book.

Transfer the required miles from your preferred partner: Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant transfer), Amex Membership Rewards (typically 1-2 business days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant to 24 hours), or Bilt (1-2 days). Always confirm availability before transferring.

Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Provide the specific flight number, date, and route you found on delta.com. The agent will search for the same availability and quote the mileage cost from Virgin's fixed award chart. Confirm the booking and pay taxes and fees.

Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart prices Delta One flights based on distance. Transatlantic routes (US to Europe) typically cost 47,500 to 60,000 Virgin miles one-way in business class. Transpacific routes cost more, around 60,000 to 80,000 miles. Compare this to Delta SkyMiles, which can charge 200,000 to 500,000 miles for the same seats.

No. As of 2026, Virgin Atlantic does not support online booking for Delta partner awards. You must call Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club phone line to book. Search for availability on delta.com first, then call with the specific flight details. The call typically takes 10-15 minutes.

Delta One is the business class cabin available on multiple aircraft types with lie-flat seats but no closing door. Delta One Suites are only on the A350-900 and feature a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a wider seat, and a more private experience. When booking, verify the aircraft type is A350-900 to ensure you get the Suite product.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Virgin Atlantic are instant. Citi ThankYou points are also fast, typically completing within minutes to 24 hours. Amex Membership Rewards and Bilt usually take 1-2 business days. Capital One transfers take 1-2 days as well. If you find availability and need to book quickly, Chase is the best source.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Booking Delta One Suites through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is the definitive workaround for Delta's punishing dynamic pricing. Paying 50,000 transferable points for a seat that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles is one of the largest arbitrage opportunities in travel rewards. The fully enclosed suite with a closing door is the best international business class product any US carrier offers. Yes, you need to call to book — but that 15-minute phone call saves you 300,000 miles. Build your transferable points balances with Chase, Amex, or Bilt, search delta.com for A350 availability, and let Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart do the rest.

#8998. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman)

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my big shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

“I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev said, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he said. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

“There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the plans because of those doubts.”

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

“That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”

Sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”

And for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

“To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

“I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before big races.”

The day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

“When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

“I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”

That feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”

Thankfully for him, time went by quickly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

After that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”

Recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”

Starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a new world’s best time, the specter of the Big Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”

One of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his new, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of new cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”

When you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”

A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev quickly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

“I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”

The bike offered another potential saving.

“My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

“Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”

#8997. Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

Lab safety scores matter, but so do fit, ventilation, and price. Here’s how the top lids compare.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

“The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
