#8965. From the Brooks Ghost 18 to Adidas Adizero Evo SL, These Are the 10 Best Men’s Running Shoes We Recommend

From road to trail, daily training to racing, these are our top trainers for every kind of runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

New runners always ask me, “What’s the best running shoe?” But there’s truly not one trainer that outperforms them all. Instead of recommending one single shoe, I consider the runner’s experience level and what they’re training for.

Maybe you signed up for your first 5K or you’re a more experienced runner setting your sights on training for your first marathon. Or maybe you’re trying to get faster or just want a new pair of kicks to start run/walking. From beginner to vet, road to trail, neutral to stability, there’s a shoe out there for everyone.

Men kind of have the upper hand in terms of running shoes because most models are designed for men’s feet by default. Even on unisex racing shoes, runners with smaller ankles (typically women) often need to use special tricks like the heel lock lacing technique to tighten the fit because they were built based on a men’s last with a wider collar.

That doesn’t mean you can zone out when it comes to finding the best fit. We have a handy guide to help you find your approximate size before shopping. There’s also width to consider, as well as intention: Do you want a grippy, durable trail shoe or a lightweight trainer for tempo runs?

Here, we break it down for you by naming our top 10 running shoes for men and provide guidance on what features you should consider.

Looking for a solid daily trainer → Nike Pegasus 42Searching for a mileage monster → New Balance EllipseA new runner → Brooks Ghost 18Adding speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLA run/walker → On Cloudmonster 3An overpronator → Saucony Guide 19Injury-prone → Saucony Triumph 24Needing a wider fit → Hoka Clifton 11Racing a marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5Hitting the trailhead → Altra Experience Wild 3

I’ve chosen to highlight each of these shoes based on feedback from the men on our editorial team, as well as the Runner’s World wear-tester program. We frequently update the lineup to ensure we're giving you the best, most up-to-date recommendations for every type of run—and runner.

Please note: While we’re experts at vetting the best footwear and update these lists often, retailer prices and stock fluctuate constantly. Our recommendations may not always be available in a given size or color. We’ll do our best to update our links to make sure you can get every pick as often as possible.

The Peg is back—and our testing proves it was worth the wait. The newest iteration is snappier and more responsive, thanks to a full-length Air Zoom unit that had one tester say, “the design leans into speed.” The shoe is a major improvement compared to its predecessor, which wasn’t necessarily bad; the Peg 41’s ride was just a little lackluster according to our testers’ feedback.

Nike stepped in to make sure the Pegasus 42 would have more rebound. The last is also modified to accommodate wider feet.

“The Nike Pegasus 42 is a solid and stable everyday trainer. Back in 1990 when I was running cross country in high school, my very first shoe was the Nike Air Pegasus and they have made some excellent changes over the past 35 years,” said tester Steven Blasi.

“The Pegasus 42 is nothing like my Pegasus from my high school days,” he continued. “The shoe is not too hard, not too soft, it is just right. The slight rocker bottom of the shoe made for a nice and smooth transition from heel to forefoot and the [Air Zoom unit] added the extra push.”

With the Ellipse you get an affordable model that packs incredible comfort and bounce. New Balance Senior Global Project Manager Paul Zielinski explained to Runner’s World how the brand set out to capture the communal aspect of our sport in a shoe. Think of the Ellipse as your “running group model,” the shoe’s ride meant to embody the rush of going on a fun run with friends.

The shoe has a retooled version of the brand’s Fresh Foam X; it has new geometry to make it springier. Though the shoe feels slightly bulky—it’s not intended for speedwork—its midsole produces a trampoline-like bounce that energizes your run.

“I like the foam,” said shoe tester and Director of News Andrew Daniels. “Some of the shoes I ran in most recently feel more firm than these, like a gym mat. This isn’t *super* sponge-y, but more in that sweet spot of just-right firm and just-right squishy, where it stays pretty bouncy for most of the run and provides good cushioning on the landings.”

Our men and women testers were split on the Ghost 18. Men liked the shoe’s ride and comfy fit, saying that even though the foam isn’t as responsive as other daily trainers they’ve tested, the Ghost 18 is a reliable shoe for logging easy workouts.

“[The Ghost 18] is well-cushioned, especially in the heel,” said Photo Director John Hamilton. “Really noticed it on a long downhill at the end of a longer run. The foam was supportive and adequate especially for slower paces but lacked a ‘pop’ when picking up the pace.”

Hamilton also noted the toe area felt slightly narrow and that a wider width would remedy this hitch (the shoe is available in wide and extra wide, as well as narrow widths).

On the other end, the air mesh upper was uncomfortable for our women testers, who complained they got hot spots under the big toe area. It’s funny to say an iteration of a shoe works better for men’s feet, but that seems to be the case with our testing—which is why the Ghost 18 made this list as Best Daily Trainer.

“I really like easy cruising, when I lay back on my heel and float,” said Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “I think that’s where this shoe works best, and probably why it’s going to work for newer runners and the majority of us who heel strike.”

Dengate said in February 2025 that the Adizero Evo SL was the shoe of the year, and that he’d feast on it if something better came along. What would lead him to make such a bold claim? For starters, the Lightstrike Pro foam in its midsole is the same cushioning Adidas used in its incredibly effective competition-grade marathon shoe, the Adios Pro 4. The Evo SL drops the Pro 4’s carbon-fiber plate in favor of a nylon shank, lending stability in a more affordable way. Because of its best value attributes (you get a heckuva lot for just $150) and dynamic construction, the shoe has been a mainstay on our lists. Dengate is definitely saved from snacking on shoelaces.

The shoe has some minor drawbacks: The tongue tends to go askew mid-run, and the fit was narrow for some of our testers. These were, by the testers’ admissions, pet peeves, though. They all said they’d continue running in the shoe, especially for speedy efforts.

“I like the lightweight feel of these sneakers,” said tester Ahmad Norman. “This helps me glide and turnover my stride at a rapid pace. I can see that training in these sneakers will most certainly increase my tempo and bring down my splits per mile.”

We love the Cloudmonster 3 at any pace, from casual walks to 4:30 strides. Our testers were impressed with the firm—but soft—Helion cushioning that provided a responsive ride for almost any kind of effort.

The shoe has On’s triple-layer CloudTec cushioning, which makes the bounce and support not much of a mystery when you see the system of holes on the shoe’s rocker shape. A Speedboard promotes propulsion and smooth push-off.

“When I slid my foot into these shoes to try on at the pickup I was instantly blown away with the shear joy it was to have these shoes on my feet,” said shoe tester Dave Brattley. “Needless to say there were some high expectations for them to perform just as well during run and they didn’t disappoint! Fit and feel, check, forefoot cushioning that’s soft but you can still feel the road, check, heel cushioning while walking, check, and durability, check! There wasn’t anything that felt off about these shoes.”

The Guide 19 is basically the same—thank goodness!—as its predecessor. It features the brand’s CenterPath technology, which adds a broader base and higher sidewalls to create a more cradled fit that provides support without constriction. Wide-footed testers love how this feature also creates an accommodating fit in the midfoot.

Pwrrun foam provides max-cushioning, making the shoe suitable for long runs and recovery days. The shoe’s rocker profile promotes fast turnover.

“Like its predecessor, this shoe made me feel good before even starting my runs,” said tester Dave Block. “I just love the comfort and feel! The shoe is very soft and slips on easily. I can’t think of any other shoe that feels this great, with the possible exception of the Adidas Pureboost, but that’s going back several years.”

The Triumph 24 is a true triumph for Saucony. The max-cushioned shoe is a mere 8.8 ounces in a men’s size 9. That’s lighter than our favorite daily trainer, the Ghost 18. The shoe’s new IncrediLux foam provides an incredibly soft—but supportive—platform.

The foam also delivers high rebound, resulting in runs that start off slow then gradually go uptempo because of the shoe’s blend of comfort and high energy return.

Testers loved the fit and feel of the trainer. For runner Phil Nicolosi, it was all about the journey and not about the stats on his watch.

“I rated the Saucony Triumph 24 very highly overall because it was one of the most comfortable max-cushioned shoes I have worn,” he said. “The fit was excellent, the upper was comfortable, and the cushioning made it easy on my aging body. It was especially good for scenic, easy runs when I was not worried about pace and just wanted to enjoy being out there.”

The Clifton is the epitome of a Hoka trainer: soft and supportive cushioning; padded, comfy, accommodating upper; rocker geometry that smooths heel-to-toe transitions. Known for its max-cushioned models, Hoka released two Cliftons this year. The Clifton Pro is an amped-up version of the Clifton 11. But in terms of recommending the best men’s shoes, I’m sticking with the original Clifton.

The Clifton 11 is like running with an old friend. The daily trainer’s rep is up there with the Nike Peg and Brooks Ghost for its overall comfort and responsive ride. The shoe has a compression-molded EVA midsole (CMEVA). Even though it’s comparatively not as bouncy as other trainers with superior foams, you still get high-energy return for daily miles and excellent support running long. It’s also a favorite for run/walking.

Hoka Clifton 11 Running Review | Hoka Clifton 11 Walking Review

The shoe worn by the fastest man, Sabastian Sawe, was the Adidas Adios Pro Evo 3. That shoe sold out in record time—at a pretty penny for $500. The next best thing? The Adidas Adios Pro 5, which is about half the price and in stock now.

The Pro 5 features a new carbon form in the shoe’s midsole; in place of rods, which mapped out the pad of your foot like your metatarsals, Adidas introduces a carbon rim. According to the brand, the rim results in 12.5 percent weight savings. Our testers found the new tech even more explosive than the Pro 4. The ride is snappy and delivers an aggressive but stable bounce thanks to the updated Lightstrike Pro foam, which is slightly firmer.

Dengate praised the shoe’s performance during a speed workout—even though he got dropped. “I loved that I could feel the foam compress and load up with each footstrike, yet feel bouncy and responsive at toe-off,” he said. “These shoes wanted more than my legs could give.”

The Experience Wild 3 has supportive cushioning without limiting ground feel, 3.5mm lugs that bite into loose terrain, and a comfortable, accommodating fit that allows you to splay your toes when hitting the trail.

With a 4mm drop, it’s a good option for runners not ready to commit to zero-drop but who still want to dabble in low-drop. The upper has a protective toe sweep and gaiter attachments.

“[The Experience Wild 3] takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, plusher cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remains stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” said tester John Mikovits.

The shoe is also available with a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Fit and comfort go hand-in-hand. You don’t want to constantly think of how loose or tight your shoes feel as you run. We recommend looking for a thumbnail’s width of toe room between the tip of your longest toe and the nose of the shoe, which leaves space for your feet to swell as you run.

Generally speaking, your running shoe should be a half size up compared to your regular street shoes. When in doubt, I generally recommend going in for a fitting and getting expert help so you're sure you find your perfect size.

Be mindful of heel rubbing and slipping. You can use the heel lock lacing technique for a snugger fit around the collar. Some runners have a high instep as well. If you feel pressure in the lacing area, you may need a shoe with a wider width.

It’s normal to have some pronation as you run. If your foot rolls excessively inward, however, you may be susceptible to knee and lower back injuries. See a specialist, like a podiatrist or physical therapist, for a gait evaluation. Special insoles and shoes with medial posts can help severe overpronators with erratic foot rolling.

If you have mild pronation or late-onset pronation, some stability shoes have holistic features, like guide rails, that act as subtle bumpers to help you when your form gets sloppy.

We recommend the Brooks Ghost 18 for beginner runners because it provides Goldilocks cushioning: not too soft, nor too hard. It’s a great starting point to see if you sway firm and lightweight or soft and max-cushioned.

Runners prefer lightweight shoes with a thinner midsole for faster efforts. These past years, however, have proven you don’t have to sacrifice stack height for speed thanks to the arrival of super foams. Still, some runners may prefer a simpler, more grounded lightweight racing flat for track workouts or hard tempos.

Max-cushioned trainers are great for long runs and recovery runs postrace, when you’re gradually adding miles again after taking time off from running.

Why should I pay more than $200 for a pair of running shoes?

Top-of-the-line running shoes made for competition feature premium materials, which generally force their prices well over the $200 line. Super foams enhance the running experience; paired with a carbon-fiber plate, this combination can improve your running economy.

These shoes are an investment and a novelty. Not everyone will experience a “4 percent” improvement. And even though super shoes eight years later are made of more durable materials (the recommended usage used to be 100 miles per pair), shelf life is still dependent on the wearer and their wear pattern.

You can also find top quality shoes for a lesser price. Training shoes, like the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6, are constructed with premium foams and have a much lower price tag than their carbon-fiber counterparts.

Can a running shoe actually make me faster?

When Nike released the original Vaporfly in 2017, many runners misinterpreted the brand's “4 percent” claim to mean running 4 percent faster, rather than improving energy efficiency. The combination of responsive super foam with a carbon-fiber plate to work as a stabilizer (the plate actually works in tandem with the foam and isn’t the root cause for propulsion) helps the wearer run more efficiently, using less oxygen and less energy to maintain their speed.

Regardless of what a brand claims, though, the only universal truth about a shoe’s impact on running performance is that no two runners will see the same benefits. A shoe is a tool: It can help you train to become stronger and improve your stride. Lightweight shoes with responsive foams can make you feel swifter and deliver more rebound, but you are the one getting faster.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8964. Is Your AI Strength Plan Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day plan complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

It all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the plan to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she says. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she says. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:

Calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold says. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold says. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

So if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the plan asks you to do them.

To its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A plan that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

ChatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

“Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

The big, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold says, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

Follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

“Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold says. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:

Core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

Unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

In race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

One last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re new to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”

Yet technique is only part of what a generic plan misses.

“Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold says. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength plan will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”

None of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a plan that wasn’t written with you in mind.

#8962. The 10 Best Trail Running Shoes for Trails, Gravel, and More

Impeccable traction and responsive rides await. These are the shoes we lace up before hitting the trailhead.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

This year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I plan on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as new shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

For over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

The Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the issues of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, new midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

Stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s issues.

Vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; new foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and says that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she says.

The shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

The Pulsar Trail has a stable ride; it’s plush underfoot and has Salomon’s signature snug fit. Road-to-trail types will love the smooth pavement transitions. It’s perfect for gravel or mixed surfaces from our earlier breakdown.

Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

Uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

Trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

Drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

Gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

#8959. This is What Happens When You Slow Down Long Enough to Be Curious

It’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions. It’s an entirely different thing to know how to slow down. Longtime mindfulness teacher, yoga therapist, and author Jillian Pransky addresses that disconnect in her recent book, The Power of the Pause: 90 Seconds to Calm, Reset, and Reconnect. In its pages, she explains exactly how pausing can alchemize everyday interactions in ways you’ve probably never considered. The following excerpt from the “Pausing in Our Discomfort Zone” chapter shows how slowing down can help you experience a more nuanced understanding of not only yourself but those who approach the world from a different perspective than you—and why that can benefit everyone. —Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ

Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone. The ability to build new neural pathways is called neuroplasticity, and it happens not only from repeating “new” behaviors, but also when we reach beyond what we know and explore new territories. Whether learning a new skill or facing a fear, your brain actively creates new neural connections, enhancing cognitive abilities, memory, and overall brain health.

However, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling. These assumptions can keep us stuck in patterns of behaviors or relationship dynamics that simply strengthen our resistance to change. When we remind ourselves that we have space to change, we often begin to see that there might be more going on than we think. We can open up to paradox, contradiction, and complexity in ways we were not able to before.

We may realize that no way is the only way. That we don’t need to make anything one way. And that things don’t always have to be precisely the way we want them.

Pausing helps us create support and safety for ourselves, giving us the confidence and courage to go beyond our comfort zone. Gradually titrating, step-by-step, into new territory allows our brain to integrate these changes, leading to our personal growth and evolution.

Dr. Gail Parker, psychologist, international presenter, and author of the self-care book Restorative Yoga for Ethnic and Race-Based Stress and Trauma, emphasizes that curiosity is essential for opening space in our conversations for connection, particularly among disparate groups of people.

She says, “You can make someone else feel safe when you are curious rather than judgmental, assuming, or indifferent. In the face of listening to others, especially those we don’t know so well or those from another culture, it’s important to remember that we can’t know everything about others or every culture, but what we can do is be curious about others.”

Listening includes being aware of ourselves and how we feel while conversing with another. In this way, we can learn to notice our own expectations and emotions, stay curious about ourselves, and hold space for ourselves and the other person. Dr. Parker suggests Pausing to check in with ourselves during conversations, with questions like:

• Am I truly listening? • Am I making assumptions? • Do I have expectations? • What am I feeling?

If we can stay aware of ourselves and curious about our feelings, we won’t get stuck in what we are feeling. “A key to remember is that if we can notice when we are in the stress response, we are not stuck in it,” she says.

Hala Khouri, author of several books, co-editor of Practicing Liberation: Transformative Strategies for Collective Healing and Systems Change, and co-founder of the social activism organization Off the Mat, Into the World, also emphasizes curiosity as an essential cornerstone for connection in difficult conversations.

Khouri, who is also a therapist, yoga teacher, and somatic experience practitioner, contends that curiosity is not only a portal for going deeper into our conversations, but is also the key to helping us know when it is time to leave a conversation—or not have one at all.

“When we are in conversation with another, I think it is important to ask ourselves, can I be curious right now? If we can’t get curious, that might be a good indicator that we need a break or need to remove ourselves from the conversation or situation, if that is an option,” she says.

The main point is that we need to stay connected to ourselves so we can sense our internal state. True listening requires curiosity. If we can’t be curious, that’s essential information for us. And, when we are highly activated in the stress response, we cannot simultaneously be curious. That part of our brain is not accessible when we are in fight-or-flight mode.

Whenever you notice you can’t be curious, take a moment to Pause and care for yourself until you can get your curiosity back.

If we could consciously choose to enter conversations with the intention to Listen—to be curious—to understand the other person’s experience a little bit better, maybe even put ourselves in their shoes, we might be able to learn from people in our lives whose world views are different from ours or even opposed to ours.

It can be helpful to remember that leading with curiosity rather than certainty doesn’t automatically mean that someone else is right. Or that we are wrong. But it opens a space in which we might connect rather than shut down to each other. The goal is not necessarily to reach agreement with others, but to understand each other. For many, this is a radical idea.

Dr. Parker emphasizes that harmonious relationships require awareness, not agreement. In fact, insisting on an agreement can be a hostile act. She says that the search for agreement can often lead to arguments because it invalidates the other person’s perspective, whereas the search for understanding dissolves the barriers that result in discord and harm and allows us to get to know one another.

She explained it like this: “If I need to be right, then I’m not going to be able to listen to you unless you are in agreement with me. And, if I need to be right, it means either you have to agree with me or you’re wrong. The need to be right means that somebody else has to be wrong. Who likes to be wrong? Nobody. Nobody wants to be made to feel like they’re wrong. Making someone wrong will most likely push them into a protective stance. But, when we approach someone with curiosity, it creates a whole new opening to make a connection with each other. We might say to them, ‘Tell me more…I’m really interested in that…I never thought about it that way.’”

When we are in difficult or uncomfortable conversations, can we create space to listen to each other with our differences? Can we create space for communication and connection for its own sake rather than for someone to be right and another to be wrong? How can we learn to understand each other rather than agree? How can we treat each other (and ourselves) better while learning to better understand each other and our different perspectives?

Pausing with the intention to prioritize Listening before speaking helps us regulate our nervous system so that we can not only create this space, but we are also less likely to activate someone else’s stress response. Khouri says, “Imagine two nervous systems on high alert trying to have a conversation, it’s almost impossible! Especially if both parties are vying for being right. If you want to disrupt that pattern, you need to figure out how to self-regulate; part of that is about tolerating the discomfort of disagreeing with someone or being in conflict.”

“One of the most interesting things I’ve discovered in my work, is that when people feel really, really listened to, they themselves are more willing to try to understand the other person, even when they don’t agree,” continues Khouri. “Through this type of listening, I’ve seen some people with very strong convictions and beliefs loosen their grip on their own fixed ideas and start to open up their perspective or get greater understanding and empathy for a different perspective.”

If we can Pause during a contentious situation and shift into curiosity, we might stay in the conversation long enough to ask questions that help us get to know someone, and listen in a way that makes them feel genuinely heard. When people feel heard and acknowledged, they are more likely to feel safe enough to listen in return. If we want to be heard and understood, it often starts with ensuring that the other person feels heard first. This of course takes practice.

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

World of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

Now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt

This is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book

Hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Before searching for availability, confirm your points position. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards and check your combined UR balance across all eligible cards. Remember, points from Chase Ink cards can be pooled with your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred. You'll need at least 25,000 points per night you want to book — a five-night trip requires 125,000 points. If you're close but not there, set a target date 3–4 months out and focus earning in the meantime.

Go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:

For adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

Return to hyatt.com, log into your World of Hyatt account, and complete the award booking for your confirmed dates. At checkout, select points as your payment method. You'll pay only minimal government taxes (typically $10–25/night). Keep your confirmation email — it will specify that the all-inclusive meals, beverages, and activities are included.

Award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

The math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

Let's walk through a real family booking so you can see exactly how the numbers work.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

The CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

The Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Book at the 395-Day Window for Peak Dates

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability

Don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further

If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

The fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively

Some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

The ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, plan for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

This redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Log into your World of Hyatt account and search for all-inclusive properties at your desired destination. Filter by the Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) or Hyatt Zilara (adults-only) brands. Check the nightly points rate — it will show the standard award rate and whether peak or off-peak pricing applies.

Check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

Complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

You can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

Most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

#8955. The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

Glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty)

For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

“Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.)

When we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly important for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

While running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global)

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

#8953. Physical Therapists Share the Most Effective QL Stretches and Exercises for Runners With Lower Back and Hip Pain

Here’s how to rehab this deep lower back muscle at home—and when it’s time to book a session with your PT.

Most runners are familiar with the big muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

If this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew says. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a big, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can issues in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas says.

Keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas says. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”

A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great issues if left unchecked. A big one? Compromised running mechanics.

A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew says. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

On top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew says.

Plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

The pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Important caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

To start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

This exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

This exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further issues arise, Agnew explains.

Jenny is a Boulder, Colorado-based health and fitness journalist. She’s been freelancing for Runner’s World since 2015 and especially loves to write human interest profiles, in-depth service pieces and stories that explore the intersection of exercise and mental health. Her work has also been published by SELF, Men’s Journal, and Condé Nast Traveler, among other outlets. When she’s not running or writing, Jenny enjoys coaching youth swimming, rereading Harry Potter, and buying too many houseplants.

#8952. Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”

The big highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a new, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

World Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this new plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the big carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

With these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations announced, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more quickly, which can be customized for various applications.

I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

These new units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).
